summary: Lit in September 1916 on Kayak Island's southwest end; the Coast Guard automated it in 1974 and a Lightkeepers Association leases the buildings.

structures.type: square concrete tower on the corner of the fog-signal building

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds open per LighthouseFriends; the dwelling and tower are closed. Visits are arranged through the Lightkeepers Association, which holds the buildings on lease.

stay.note: Bunks for as many as 10 paying visitors; book through the association.

events.note: Act of 22 Oct 1913 appropriated $115,000 for a light and fog signal
Construction began 1 June 1915 (Commissioner); the nomination says early 1915
6 September 1916 per the Service; the 1975 nomination gives 16 September
Gas, whistling and bell buoy No. 2 went adrift in a strong southeast gale, 13 Sept 1918; not recovered by 1920
Replacement buoy placed off the cape in June 1919 was lost; found ashore on Elizabeth Island
Radio beacon installed at the station
Brown bear tried to enter the keepers' residence (LighthouseFriends)
Good Friday earthquake; rockfall and tsunami; a Coast Guard crew member drowned (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard notice to automate five Alaskan lights, including this one
Fresnel lens removed from the tower sometime before 1973; replaced by a smaller beacon
Unmanned and downgraded to a minor light
Cape St. Elias Lightkeepers Association organized; 30-year lease from the Coast Guard

corrections.why: Two OSM-sourced structure rows give 1816 as the build date, and an 1816 event is listed. Both the 1975 nomination and the Commissioner's reports date the station to 1915 to 1916 construction; no source checked supports 1816.
The nomination says the light was displayed forty feet above high water (12.2 m). The record's 25.9 m is not supported by any source checked.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination says Congress approved the station in 1911 and funded it in October 1913. The Commissioner's report for 1915 shows the appropriation was the act of 22 October 1913.

notes_for_editor: Keeper roster matched by name and establishment year (1916) only: the USLHS place record puts Cape St. Elias at 60 deg 9.48 min N, 146 deg 50.12 min W, about 131 km from the station's coordinates, so the archive's place coordinates are wrong and the roster should be checked against the place page. LighthouseFriends prints the same roster and gives 59.79841, -144.59886 for the map; the record's coordinates agree with that. Disagreements left open in the story: first-lit date (6 vs 16 September 1916), construction start (early 1915 vs 1 June 1915), dwelling material (reinforced concrete per the nomination vs bricks per LighthouseFriends, which lists the keepers' dwelling among the brick buildings), candlepower (300,000 per the Commissioner's report and LighthouseFriends vs 390 per the nomination), range (LighthouseFriends prints a fraction after '15' that the cached copy shows only as a replacement character, so the story says 'about 15 nautical miles'; the nomination says visible about eleven miles), and lantern and lens order. The 1964 drowning and the 1961 bear incident come from LighthouseFriends alone; no second source was checked for them. The focal height is from the nomination ('forty feet above high water', 12.2 m); the record's 25.9 m is unsupported (see corrections). The tower's height and build date are not in any source checked, so the JSON gives type and material only. The association website calls the station a National Historic Landmark; no source checked confirms that, so the story does not say it. LighthouseFriends' data sheet says Open to Public: Yes, but its visitor notes say grounds open, dwelling and tower closed; the story follows the visitor notes. Omitted on purpose: LighthouseFriends' accounts of a construction-camp cook's death and a 1962 crew incident (personal detail, not about the station's work). The station's record shows characteristic Fl W 10s and 14 nm; neither is confirmed by a source checked here, so the JSON leaves the characteristic out.
